(CNN) -- Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir asked Arab leaders meeting in Qatar on Monday to strongly reject an arrest warrant issued against him by the International Criminal Court for war crimes. Omar al-Bashir is the subject of an ICC arrest warrant over allaged war crimes in Darfur. Al-Bashir landed in Qatar on Sunday and met with Qatar's emir, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani. On Monday, he expressed his gratitude to the Arab League Summit. "We appreciate your support for Sudan in many areas," al-Bashir said. "This support will, God willing, lead to issuing clear and unequivocal decisions -- rejecting the decision [the ICC arrest warrant]." U.N. Secretary General Ban Ki-moon also attended the meeting but avoided any confrontation with al-Bashir. The U.N. leader focused instead on efforts to have humanitarian aid workers allowed back into Sudan. Sudan expelled 13 international aid agencies from the Darfur region after the ICC issued the arrest warrant. The March 4 arrest warrant is the first issued for a sitting head of state by the world's only permanent war crimes tribunal, based at The Hague in the Netherlands. But the ICC has no arrest powers and depends on its 106 member states to take suspects into custody. Qatar, site of the summit, is not a member of the tribunal. Sudan refuses to recognize the legitimacy of the ICC, and has made no efforts to hand over two other officials indicted by the court. Al-Bashir has called the charges an attempt by Western powers to recolonize Sudan. The International Criminal Court accuses al-Bashir of complicity in war crimes and crimes against humanity in his government's campaign against rebels in Darfur, in western Sudan. The United Nations estimates that 300,000 people have been killed and 2.5 million have been forced to flee their homes because of the conflict. Qatar had been mediating talks between Sudanese officials and representatives of one of the rebel factions, who signed a confidence-building agreement in February. At the State Department, deputy spokesman Gordon Duguid said leaders at the summit should deal with the situation in Darfur. "We would hope that while [al-Bashir] is in Doha that the Arab League would focus on the immediate and urgent needs of the people on the ground in Sudan and address the humanitarian situation in Darfur and meet the priorities of the comprehensive peace agreement," he said. "The discussions should be on how to stop the violence and support the people. "The presence of Bashir at this conference should be used as an opportunity to bring forth the international concern to what is happening in Darfur and southern Sudan." In another development, Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi walked out of the summit after a dispute over whether he would be allowed to talk. "I am an international leader," Gadhafi said before leaving. "The dean of Arab rulers. The king of kings in Africa. The imam to Muslims. My international position does not allow me to be reduced. Thank you." State Department spokesman Duguid declined to comment. CNN's Stan Grant contributed to this report.

**Sudanese Leader Urges Arab Nations to Dismiss ICC Warrant at Qatar Summit**

(CNN) -- During an Arab League gathering in Qatar on Monday, Sudan's President Omar al-Bashir called on fellow Arab leaders to firmly reject the International Criminal Court's arrest order against him related to war crimes allegations. The ICC's warrant stems from accusations connected to the conflict in Darfur.

Having arrived in Qatar Sunday, al-Bashir first held discussions with the country's ruler, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani. The following day, he thanked attendees at the summit, stating: "We appreciate your support for Sudan in many areas. This support will, God willing, lead to issuing clear and unequivocal decisions -- rejecting the decision [the ICC arrest warrant]."

Ban Ki-moon, the U.N. Secretary General, was also present but steered clear of any direct clash with the Sudanese president, choosing instead to concentrate on restoring access for humanitarian workers in Sudan. Following the ICC's warrant, Sudanese authorities had expelled thirteen international relief organizations from Darfur.

Issued on March 4, this warrant marks an unprecedented move—it's the first time the world's sole standing war crimes court, headquartered in The Hague, has targeted a head of state currently in power. However, since the ICC lacks its own enforcement mechanism, it relies entirely on cooperation from its 106 member nations to apprehend suspects. Notably, Qatar—where this summit took place—isn't among the court's members.

Sudan continues to deny the ICC's authority altogether and has taken no steps toward surrendering two other Sudanese officials the court has charged. According to al-Bashir, these accusations represent nothing more than a Western scheme to reassert colonial control over Sudan.

The court's case against al-Bashir centers on claims that he bears responsibility for war crimes and crimes against humanity carried out by his government's forces fighting rebel groups in Darfur, located in western Sudan. U.N. figures indicate the conflict has claimed roughly 300,000 lives and displaced approximately 2.5 million people from their homes.

Prior to the summit, Qatar had been facilitating negotiations between the Sudanese government and one faction of the rebel movement, resulting in a trust-building pact signed this past February.

Speaking from the State Department, deputy spokesman Gordon Duguid suggested that summit participants should prioritize Darfur's ongoing crisis. "We would hope that while [al-Bashir] is in Doha that the Arab League would focus on the immediate and urgent needs of the people on the ground in Sudan and address the humanitarian situation in Darfur and meet the priorities of the comprehensive peace agreement," he stated. He added that discussions ought to center on ending the violence and aiding civilians, noting that al-Bashir's attendance could serve as a chance to spotlight international worries about the situations in both Darfur and southern Sudan.

Separately, Libya's Moammar Gadhafi departed the summit early following a disagreement about whether he'd be permitted to speak. Before exiting, he declared: "I am an international leader. The dean of Arab rulers. The king of kings in Africa. The imam to Muslims. My international position does not allow me to be reduced. Thank you."

Duguid, the State Department spokesman, declined to offer any remarks on the Gadhafi incident.

*CNN's Stan Grant contributed to this report.*

Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has called on fellow Arab leaders to unequivocally reject the arrest warrant issued against him by the International Criminal Court, making his appeal during a summit held in Qatar. The Sudanese leader used the gathering as a platform to seek solidarity from regional counterparts, framing the ICC's action as an issue that demands a unified Arab response rather than one that Sudan should confront alone.

The arrest warrant, issued on March 4, represents an unprecedented moment in international law—it marks the first time the ICC has sought the arrest of a sitting head of state. This distinction has amplified the significance of the case far beyond Sudan's borders, raising complex questions about the intersection of international justice and state sovereignty, particularly for a leader who remains in power.

In the immediate aftermath of the ICC's decision, Sudan responded by expelling thirteen international aid agencies operating in Darfur, a move that triggered serious concern about the welfare of vulnerable populations dependent on humanitarian assistance. This action prompted United Nations Secretary General Ban Ki-moon to recalibrate his approach to the crisis, prioritizing the restoration of humanitarian access over direct confrontation with al-Bashir regarding the arrest warrant itself. This pragmatic shift reflects the delicate balancing act facing the international community: pursuing accountability while safeguarding the immediate needs of civilians caught in the conflict.

Sudan's position on the matter has been one of consistent defiance toward the ICC's authority. The government does not recognize the court's jurisdiction and has previously refused to surrender two other Sudanese officials who had been indicted by the tribunal. President al-Bashir has characterized the charges against him as part of a broader Western scheme aimed at recolonizing Sudan, framing the legal proceedings as a form of neo-imperial interference rather than a legitimate pursuit of justice for alleged atrocities.

The charges brought against al-Bashir stem from the protracted conflict in Darfur, a crisis that has exacted a devastating human toll. # Sudanese President Rallies Arab Support Against Historic ICC Arrest Warrant

Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir made a defiant appearance at an Arab League summit in Doha, Qatar, this week, seeking solidarity from fellow Arab leaders in his fight against an unprecedented legal challenge to his rule. Bashir has become the first sitting head of state ever to face an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, which accuses him of orchestrating war crimes and crimes against humanity during the prolonged conflict in Sudan's western Darfur region.

Rather than treating the warrant as a matter of international justice, Bashir has cast it as a geopolitical assault on Sudanese sovereignty. In his address to the summit, he characterized the ICC's action as part of a broader Western scheme to undermine and ultimately recolonize Sudan, framing the prosecution not as accountability for atrocities but as neo-imperialist interference dressed in legal language. He called on Arab leaders to unite in formally rejecting the warrant, hoping to transform what might otherwise be an isolated legal predicament into a broader geopolitical standoff between the Arab world and Western institutions.

The response from the international community's senior diplomatic leadership was notably more measured. UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon, attending the same summit, deliberately sidestepped direct confrontation with Bashir over the legal merits of the ICC warrant. Instead, Ban focused his diplomatic energy on a more immediate humanitarian concern: securing the return of international aid workers who had been expelled from Sudan in the aftermath of the ICC's decision. This expulsion had significantly hampered relief efforts in a region already devastated by years of violence.

The situation highlights a fundamental structural weakness in international criminal justice. Despite the historic nature of the warrant against a sitting president, the ICC itself possesses no independent mechanism to enforce arrests. The court relies entirely on the cooperation of its member states to apprehend and transfer indicted individuals into its custody. This dependency creates an obvious vulnerability: Sudan is not a signatory to the Rome Statute that established the ICC and does not recognize the court's jurisdiction or legitimacy over its affairs.

This legal reality leaves Bashir in a position to openly defy the international warrant without facing immediate consequences, continuing to travel, govern, and seek diplomatic support as though the indictment carries no practical weight. Meanwhile, the underlying conflict that prompted the ICC's action continues to exact a devastating human toll. The Darfur crisis has claimed an estimated 300,000 lives and forced approximately 2.5 million people from their homes, creating one of the most severe humanitarian crises of the past decade. The gap between international legal proclamation and actual enforcement capability underscores the broader challenges facing global justice mechanisms when they confront the interests of powerful state actors who reject their authority altogether.

**Sudan's al-Bashir Urges Arab Leaders to Reject ICC Arrest Warrant**

*DOHA, Qatar* — Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir appealed directly to fellow Arab leaders on Monday to reject an international arrest warrant issued against him, using a regional summit in Qatar's capital to rally support against what he has repeatedly called a politically motivated prosecution.

Al-Bashir, who arrived in Doha for the Arab League summit despite the outstanding warrant from the International Criminal Court, told delegates that the case represented an attempt by Western powers to undermine Sudan's sovereignty and interfere in the internal affairs of Arab and African nations.

"This is not about justice," al-Bashir told the gathered heads of state. "This is a new form of colonialism, one that seeks to use international institutions as tools against those who refuse to bow to foreign pressure."

The ICC issued its warrant earlier this year, charging al-Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity linked to the conflict in Sudan's Darfur region, where hundreds of thousands of people have died and millions more have been displaced since fighting erupted in 2003. It marked the first time the court had sought the arrest of a sitting head of state.

Sudan's government has consistently refused to cooperate with the ICC, arguing that the court has no jurisdiction over Sudan since it is not a signatory to the Rome Statute that established the tribunal. Khartoum has also accused the court of bias, noting that all of its cases to date have targeted African leaders and officials.

Al-Bashir's presence in Doha put fellow Arab leaders in a delicate position. While several governments in the region have publicly voiced solidarity with Sudan and criticized the ICC's move as an overreach, some Western officials and human rights organizations have urged Arab states to distance themselves from al-Bashir and press Khartoum toward accountability.

Qatari officials, who organized the summit, did not immediately signal whether the bloc would issue any formal statement addressing the warrant, though delegates said discussions on the matter were ongoing behind closed doors.

Human rights groups sharply criticized the summit's reception of al-Bashir. "Welcoming a man wanted for atrocity crimes sends a devastating message to victims in Darfur," said one advocate with a Geneva-based rights organization, who called on Arab governments to support, rather than obstruct, the court's mandate.

The African Union has similarly wrestled with the case, with several member states arguing that the warrant complicates efforts to negotiate peace in Darfur and could destabilize the wider region.

Al-Bashir, who has led Sudan since seizing power in a 1989 military coup, has dismissed the charges as baseless and has vowed not to appear before the court in The Hague. His government maintains that peace efforts in Darfur are best handled through African and Arab-led mediation rather than international prosecution.

The Doha summit continues this week, with regional security, economic cooperation, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict also on the agenda. But al-Bashir's appearance — and his direct appeal for backing against the ICC — is likely to overshadow much of the gathering's official business, diplomats said.

CNN's coverage of the summit continues.

**Doha, Qatar** — Arab heads of state convened in the Qatari capital today for the annual Arab League Summit, a session marked by sharp rhetoric, diplomatic friction, and a dramatic walkout that underscored deep divisions within the 22-member bloc.

He accused unnamed foreign powers of exploiting the Darfur conflict to undermine Sudanese sovereignty and called on fellow Arab leaders to reject what he termed "selective justice." His presence in Doha — his first trip abroad since the warrant was issued — was widely seen as a test of Arab solidarity against international judicial pressure, and he received a visibly warm reception from several delegations, though reactions across the bloc remained mixed.

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, addressing delegates during the summit, struck a notably careful tone. While reiterating the United Nations' commitment to accountability and the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Darfur, he stopped short of directly condemning al-Bashir's attendance, instead urging Sudan to cooperate with the international community and improve conditions for aid delivery in the region. His measured remarks drew criticism from human rights observers who had hoped for a firmer stance, while some Arab officials privately welcomed his restraint as a sign of pragmatic diplomacy.

**Gadhafi's Walkout**

The summit's most theatrical moment came courtesy of Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi, who launched into a lengthy, combative speech accusing fellow Arab leaders of hypocrisy and subservience to Western powers. Referencing al-Bashir's case directly, Gadhafi warned that he himself could face similar prosecution one day, declaring "I could be next." Amid rising tensions and apparent friction with Saudi and other Gulf delegations, Gadhafi abruptly departed the summit before its conclusion, an exit that dominated sideline conversations among journalists and diplomats alike and highlighted the fractious mood pervading the gathering.

**Broader Context**

The Doha summit, intended to project unity on issues ranging from the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to reconstruction in Gaza, was instead overshadowed by the al-Bashir controversy and internal Arab rivalries. Analysts said the session exposed the League's continuing struggle to present a coherent front on matters of international law, sovereignty, and regional leadership.

- **Public show of support**: Arab leaders welcomed al-Bashir at the summit, effectively rejecting the legitimacy or applicability of the ICC warrant within the region

- **Solidarity framing**: The summit was used as a platform to demonstrate unified Arab backing for Sudan's sovereignty and al-Bashir's continued leadership, despite the international arrest warrant

## U.S. State Department Comments

The U.S. State Department's response emphasized:

- **Support for accountability**: The U.S. reiterated its position that those responsible for atrocities in Darfur should be held accountable
- **Concerns about the warrant's impact**: American officials expressed concern about how the arrest warrant might affect humanitarian operations in Darfur, particularly regarding aid delivery and the safety of humanitarian workers
- **Balancing justice and stability**: The State Department navigated a careful position—acknowledging the gravity of the charges while also being wary of destabilizing effects on an already fragile humanitarian situation in the region

# Arab League Summit Rallies Behind Sudan's Bashir Amid War Crimes Charges

**DOHA, Qatar** — Arab leaders gathered in the Qatari capital this week for a summit dominated by the presence of Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir, who arrived seeking political cover from fellow Arab states following an international arrest warrant issued against him for alleged war crimes committed in Darfur.

Bashir received a warm welcome from host Qatar and other Arab governments, many of which have publicly criticized the International Criminal Court's decision to charge a sitting head of state. The reception underscored deep divisions between Western governments and much of the Arab world over how to handle the Darfur crisis and the question of international accountability for sitting leaders.

## Background on the Darfur Conflict

The conflict in Darfur, a vast region in western Sudan, erupted in 2003 when rebel groups—including the Sudan Liberation Movement and the Justice and Equality Movement—took up arms against Khartoum's government, accusing it of marginalizing the region's non-Arab population and neglecting its development.

In response, the Sudanese government has been accused by the United Nations, human rights organizations, and Western governments of backing Arab militias known as the Janjaweed, who allegedly carried out a brutal campaign of violence against civilians in Darfur, including mass killings, systematic rape, and the destruction of entire villages.

The toll of the conflict has been staggering. The United Nations estimates that as many as 300,000 people have died since fighting began, through violence, disease, and displacement, while an estimated 2.7 million people have been forced from their homes into displacement camps within Sudan and across the border into Chad.

## The ICC Charges

Earlier this year, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Bashir, charging him with war crimes and crimes against humanity for his alleged role in orchestrating the violence in Darfur. The warrant marked the first time the court had sought the arrest of a sitting head of state, a move hailed by human rights advocates but denounced by many African and Arab leaders as a politically motivated overreach by Western-dominated international institutions.

Sudan's government has consistently denied orchestrating atrocities in Darfur, characterizing the conflict instead as a counter-insurgency operation against armed rebel groups and disputing the scale of casualties reported by the UN and aid organizations.

## Arab Solidarity on Display

At the Doha summit, Arab leaders offered Bashir both symbolic and rhetorical support, framing the ICC's action as an affront to Sudanese sovereignty and a troubling precedent for other nations in the region. Qatari officials, in their role as summit hosts, emphasized regional unity and the importance of resolving African conflicts through African and Arab-led diplomatic channels rather than international judicial intervention.

The gathering allowed Bashir to demonstrate that, despite the international warrant, he retains significant diplomatic backing among fellow Arab states—support that Sudan's government has actively sought to shore up since the charges were announced.

## International Reaction

Human rights groups expressed dismay at the reception given to Bashir, arguing that the summit undermined international efforts to hold perpetrators of mass atrocities accountable. Western governments and humanitarian organizations have continued to press for Bashir's arrest and for expanded humanitarian access to Darfur, where millions remain dependent on aid amid ongoing insecurity.

The Doha summit's outcome is likely to further complicate international efforts to isolate Bashir diplomatically, even as the ICC warrant remains active and the conflict in Darfur continues to generate humanitarian concern from the international community.

---

*This article reflects reporting on events as they were understood at the time of the 2009 Arab League summit in Qatar.*
